1.e4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, mirroring White's move. Black aims for quick development and early castling, while the e5-pawn is a target that White can attack at once. Play is often open, and White keeps the first-move initiative.

1.e4 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 from the flank instead of mirroring White. If White opens the centre, Black trades a wing pawn for a central one, which gives a central majority and a half-open c-file. White usually leads in development and attacks the kingside, Black counterattacks on the queenside, and the unbalanced structure gives both sides winning chances.

1.e4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the e-pawn behind it and accepts a slightly cramped position in return for a resilient structure. The c8-bishop is hemmed in by the e6-pawn and often has to be traded or rerouted, but Black has clear plans against White's centre with ...c5. The result is a sound game, at the price of some passivity.

1.e4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop free to come out before ...e6, so Black gets a sound pawn structure without a passive light-squared bishop. The price is time: the knight loses its natural c6-square. White usually gets more space and freer development, while Black relies on a solid structure with few weaknesses.

1.e4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and trades Black's d-pawn for White's e-pawn. Black gets an open game and easy development, but recapturing costs time, so Black gives up some tempi and space for it.

1.e4 d6.strategy: Prepares to develop the knight and fianchetto the king's bishop, and invites White to build a broad centre, which Black then undermines with pawn breaks. The set-up is flexible and keeps many pawn structures possible, but White gets space and attacking chances if Black reacts passively.

1.e4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once and invites White to advance the pawn, hoping the advanced pawns become targets. White gains space and tempi by chasing the knight, and Black gets counterplay against the overextended centre. The game is double-edged.

1.e4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 to hit White's centre from a distance and keeps the choice of set-up open until White commits. Black accepts less space for a flexible set-up with counterplay later. The risk is a passive position if White builds a big centre and Black does not strike back in time.

1.e4 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence
1.e4 Nc6.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who originated the defence and usually answered 2.d4 with 2...d5. Kasparov and Keene wrote that it “has never been fully accepted as a dependable opening”, though they considered it sound.
1.e4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight at once and invites White to build a pawn centre that Black then challenges. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the usual ...c6 and ...c5 breaks are unavailable, and White keeps more space. Sound, but it gives White the easier game.

1.e4 b6.name: Owen's Defence
1.e4 b6.background: Named after John Owen, a nineteenth-century English vicar and strong amateur, who played it in two games against Paul Morphy in 1858, winning one and losing one. It was rare at master level until Bent Larsen and Michael Basman adopted it in the 1970s.
1.e4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to press on e4 and the long diagonal, but leaves the centre to White, who can build a broad pawn centre against it. Theory regards the move as unreliable rather than refuted, since the bishop's pressure seldom makes up for the space conceded.

1.e4 a6.name: St. George Defence
1.e4 a6.background: The first known game with 1.e4 a6 was a simultaneous exhibition on 11 December 1868, in which the English amateur J. Baker beat Wilhelm Steinitz. Tony Miles beat Anatoly Karpov with it at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara, after which it was also called the Birmingham Defence, after Miles's hometown.
1.e4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 to attack the centre from the flank, and keeps the choice of set-up open. White simply takes space, and the slow a-pawn move needs ...b5 to justify its tempo. Sound enough, but Black has spent a tempo and conceded the centre.

1.e4 h6.name: Carr Defence
1.e4 h6.background: The defence is mentioned in Unorthodox Chess Openings, and Michael Basman and Magnus Carlsen have both played it.
1.e4 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook's pawn to prevent Bg5 and prepare ...g5, but does nothing for the centre or development. White has a free hand in the centre, and a follow-up ...g5 only adds a weakened kingside.

1.e4 Na6.name: Lemming Defence
1.e4 Na6.strategy: Sends the knight to the edge, where it does nothing for the centre and can be exchanged by Bxa6 bxa6, which doubles the a-pawns. White takes the centre at leisure while the knight still looks for a useful square.

1.e4 Nh6.name: Adams Defence
1.e4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it covers f5 and g4 but becomes a target: after d4 the bishop on c1 can take it with Bxh6 gxh6 and wreck Black's kingside pawns. Black also spends time without helping the centre.

1.e4 a5.name: Ware Defence
1.e4 a5.background: Also known as the Corn Stalk Defence. Preston Ware, an American player who often played uncommon openings, used it in eleven recorded tournament games from 1880 to 1882, winning four and losing seven.
1.e4 a5.strategy: A rook's pawn move that neither challenges the centre nor develops a piece, and it weakens b5. White takes the centre at leisure and Black has no compensation for the lost time.

1.e4 b5.name: O'Neill Gambit
1.e4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn: 2.Bxb5 wins it at once, and the compensation, ...Bb7 against e4 and the half-open b-file, is too little, since White defends e4 easily and stays a clean pawn up.

1.e4 f6.name: Barnes Defence
1.e4 f6.background: Named after Thomas Wilson Barnes, who beat Paul Morphy with it in 1858, although it is regarded as clearly inferior.
1.e4 f6.strategy: Blocks the natural f6 square of the king's knight and weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the king. White takes the centre and develops freely, while Black has no useful follow-up.

1.e4 f5.name: Duras Gambit
1.e4 f5.background: The line was played three times in an exhibition match between Ossip Bernstein and Oldřich Duras, after whom the gambit is named.
1.e4 f5.strategy: Offers a pawn: after 2.exf5 Black gets a modest lead in development with ...Nf6 but little else for it, and the e8–h5 diagonal and the king stay weakened.

1.e4 g5.name: Borg Defence
1.e4 g5.background: The name is “Grob” spelled backwards. Michael Basman often played it, and it is also called the Basman Defence; Modern Chess Openings judges Black only somewhat worse, although the move weakens the kingside severely.
1.e4 g5.strategy: Gains kingside space at the price of a lasting weakness: after 2.d4 the bishop on c1 attacks the g5-pawn at once, and the squares around Black's king stay weak for the rest of the game.

1.e4 h5.name: Goldsmith Defence
1.e4 h5.background: Also called the Pickering Defence, it is the Kádas Opening (1.h4) with the colours reversed. Modern Chess Openings dismisses it: “Other defenses, such as 1...h5, are not considered as they are simply too bad and need no discussion.”
1.e4 h5.strategy: Wastes a tempo and weakens g5 and the whole kingside for no gain: the pawn does nothing for the centre or development, and White simply takes the centre.

1.e4.name: King's Pawn Game
1.e4.background: The most popular first move in chess. Bobby Fischer called it “best by test” in My 60 Memorable Games (1969).

1.e4 a5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once. Black's 1...a5 does nothing for development or the middle of the board, so White occupies it with a second pawn and gains space, the initiative and a free choice of set-up.

1.e4 a6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the full centre and lets Black show what 1...a6 is for. Black has chosen to attack the centre from the flank instead of occupying it, so two central pawns are the natural answer and the test of that plan.

1.e4 b6 2.d4.strategy: A principled reply: White takes space with both centre pawns, and both bishops are ready to enter the game. Black has offered the centre on purpose, so the question is whether the fianchettoed bishop can make White's big centre a target.

1.e4 f6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn. Black's f6 neither develops a piece nor fights the centre: it takes the best square from the g8 knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal against the king, and 2...e5 fails to 3.dxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+.

1.e4 g5 2.d4.strategy: Attacks the loose pawn at once: the bishop on c1 now sees g5 and nothing defends it. White takes the centre with tempo while Black's kingside pawn move has weakened the position and cost time.

1.e4 h5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and leaves Black's rook-pawn move as a wasted tempo that also weakens the kingside. White is ahead in space and development and just needs to play normally.

1.e4 h6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre against a move that develops nothing and fights for nothing. White builds a pawn centre and develops with an edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the full pawn centre at once, which is exactly what Black's last move invited. White gains space and the initiative, and Black has to prove that the centre can be undermined or restrained. This is the principled test of the whole defence.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Declined Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.background: White players not eager for a theoretical battle on their opponent's turf often choose it.
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e5 while declining the fight on Black's own ground. If Black plays ...e5 the game becomes an ordinary open one, and avoiding that means choosing a less natural set-up. White keeps the d-pawn flexible and sidesteps prepared lines.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends e4 without committing the d-pawn. Sound but unambitious: Black can occupy the centre with the e-pawn for an ordinary open game, or pick its own set-up, and White has no special edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight, hoping for a well-known pressure game if Black fills the centre with ...e5. Until then the bishop achieves little, since nothing yet depends on the knight, and Black has several comfortable ways to avoid the transposition. An offbeat try, not a threat.
1.e4 Nc6 2.Bb5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Pseudo-Spanish Variation

1.e4 Nc6 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to gain time for a broad centre. After ...Nxb4 White can drive the knight back with c3, but that leaves Black a clean pawn up in a solid position; the pawn is hard to justify.
1.e4 Nc6 2.b4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Wheeler Gambit

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the whole centre, since the knight on the rim has no useful way to attack it. White gets a freer game, and Black has to justify the odd development with counterplay later.

1.e4 a5 2.d4 Nc6.name: Ware Defence: Snagglepuss Defence
1.e4 a5 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: The first move since 1...a5 that does something useful: the knight develops and presses on d4, which the queen guards. Black still concedes the larger share of the centre and has to prove that the a-pawn move was worth the time.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5.strategy: The point of 1...a6: the a-pawn guards b5, and the b-pawn clears b7 for the bishop, which will eye e4 from the flank. Black leaves White the centre and aims to undermine it from the wing while gaining queenside space.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 e5.name: St. George Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 a6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Gives up a pawn at once: after dxe5 Black has developed nothing and has no easy way to win it back, since Nf3 holds e5. Striking at the centre before any piece is out leaves White with the easier game.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4 while keeping the c-pawn free. The natural 3.Nc3 would run into ...b4, which drives the knight away and leaves e4 without support, so the knight goes to f3 and e4 is left for the bishop to hold.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7.strategy: Develops with pressure on the undefended e4 pawn. Nc3 is not available as a defence because of ...b4, so White has to find another way to hold e4, while Black gains play along the long diagonal and on the queenside.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3.strategy: The main line: it defends e4 with a developing move, unlike Nbd2, which would block the c1-bishop. The bishop also looks at b5, guarded by the a6 pawn, and keeps White's broad centre intact while Black has to undermine it from a distance.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 e6.name: St. George Defence: Polish Variation
1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 e6.strategy: The main line: a pawn on e6 takes d5 and f5 from White, opens the dark-squared bishop and prepares quick kingside development. Black builds a compact centre of their own rather than leaving White's pawns unopposed.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6.strategy: Holds e5 for a later central break and aims for a compact structure in which Black fights the centre with the e-pawn, as in a classical set-up for the second player. It keeps the e-pawn flexible but leaves the dark-squared bishop with less scope than 4...e6.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.strategy: Puts the king to safety at once. The bishop on d3 already protects e4, so White has no worries in the centre and can finish development before deciding how to meet Black's flank play.

Prepares a second fianchetto, so that both bishops eye White's central pawns from the wings. Black concedes the centre completely and plans to undermine it from a distance, an offbeat and rather passive way to meet White's solid set-up.
Shores up d4 before the bishop on g7 can pressure it, and gives the d3-bishop the c2 retreat. It makes the centre solid but takes c3 from the b1-knight, which has to find another route.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.name: St. George Defence: San Jorge Variation
1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.strategy: Completes the double fianchetto: the bishop on g7 joins the one on b7 in aiming at White's centre, and the king can castle behind a sound pawn shield. Black is passive but safe, and every bit of play comes from undermining White's pawns.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and pressures e4, so White has to defend the pawn at once. Black lets White hold the centre on purpose and plans to attack it from a distance, with the bishop on the long diagonal and a pawn break later.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Hits the d4 pawn from the flank at once, striking at the centre before White has built it up. If White takes on c5, Black must recapture with the b-pawn, which abandons the queenside set-up chosen with 1...b6, or play a pawn down for activity.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Ba6.name: Owen's Defence: Guatemala Defence
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Ba6.background: Invented by the Guatemalan player Roberto Asturias and further investigated by his compatriots, among them David Vela and Hans Cohn.
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Ba6.strategy: Offers to trade the light-squared bishops at once, but after the trade Black's recapturing knight lands on the edge of the board and White keeps the whole centre for nothing. It leaves book quickly without solving any problem.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3.strategy: The principal answer: it guards e4 with a developing move and keeps White's broad centre intact. The bishop eyes the kingside, and Black has to work against the pawns from a distance, with White keeping a slight edge.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Nf3.name: Owen's Defence: Smith Gambit
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops but leaves e4 undefended on purpose: if Black takes it with the bishop, White hunts the bishop with tempo, hoping the lead in development repays the pawn. At best a modest pawn's worth of play, so a gamble.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bg5.name: Owen's Defence: Naselwaus Gambit
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops with a thrust at e7, which is easily defended, and leaves e4 without a defender: Black simply takes the pawn with the bishop and White has nothing to show for it. A gambit without enough compensation.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.f3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn, but takes the natural square from the g1-knight and loosens the diagonal to the king. Black gets to strike at the centre at once, so White has bought an awkward set-up for a pawn's protection.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 c5 3.dxc5.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and settles the tension. Black can recapture at once only with the b-pawn, which gives up the queenside set-up chosen with 1...b6, and otherwise has to play a pawn down for activity.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5.strategy: Loses by force: the pawn push opens the diagonal from h5 to the king on e8. White takes it, and the greedy bishop capture on g2 that Black hopes for then runs straight into a decisive queen check.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn and, with f7 gone, opens the diagonal from h5 to the king on e8. The greedy reply 4...Bxg2 walks into the queen check on h5, and White's lead in development and attack grows quickly.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5 Bxg2.strategy: Grabs a pawn and attacks the h1-rook but falls into the trap: after the check on h5 and the forced block on g6, fxg6 threatens gxh7 with a discovered check, and taking the rook even allows mate on h7.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5 Bxg2 5..strategy: Springs the trap: the queen checks along the open diagonal, the check must be blocked, and the bishop on g2 is far from the defence of the king. Black's pieces cannot meet the attack that follows.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5 Bxg2 5..name: Owen's Defence: Matovinsky Gambit
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5 Bxg2 5..background: Greco already gave the line 4.exf5 Bxg2 5.Qh5+ g6 6.fxg6 in the seventeenth century, as a refutation of 3...f5.
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 f5 4.exf5 Bxg2 5..strategy: The only legal move, and the position is already lost: fxg6 opens the lines around the king and threatens gxh7 with a discovered check, so even a developing move such as ...Nf6 runs into mate.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.f3 e5.name: Owen's Defence: Wind Gambit
1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.f3 e5.strategy: Hits the d4 pawn at once, exploiting a set-up that has taken f3 from the knight and loosened the diagonal to the king. Black opens the centre while White's pieces are awkwardly placed and White has to resolve the tension.

1.e4 b6 2.d4 c5 3.dxc5 Nc6.name: Owen's Defence: Hekili-Loa Gambit
1.e4 b6 2.d4 c5 3.dxc5 Nc6.strategy: Develops instead of recapturing: a pawn gambit for activity and open lines. White can simply take a second pawn with cxb6 and keep the extra material, so Black has to prove the compensation is real.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, where the bishop eyes e4 along the long diagonal and fights the centre from a distance. It is a sensible development idea, but f6 has already weakened the kingside, and White has the whole centre to expand against.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 Kf7.name: Fried Fox Defence
1.e4 f6 2.d4 Kf7.strategy: Walks the king to f7, giving up castling, and Bc4+ checks it at once with a gain of time. Black must block or retreat, and is left with an exposed king, a pawn centre against it and no development.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a broad centre: the c-pawn joins d4 and e4 and controls d5, so the bishop has no easy outpost. White gains space, at the price of e4 needing a piece to guard it once the bishop arrives on b7.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 Bb7.name: Owen's Defence: Unicorn Variation
1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 Bb7.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal and attacks the undefended e4 pawn at once, so White has to spend a tempo guarding it. This is the point of ...b6: Black fights the centre from a distance instead of occupying it with pawns.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6.strategy: Defends the attacked pawn with another pawn and holds on to the material. Black keeps the plan of a fianchettoed bishop but has spent two wing pawn moves with no piece out, so White's lead in development and space is the price.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.name: Borg Defence: Borg Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.strategy: Ignores the attack on g5 and hits the d4 pawn with the fianchettoed bishop. The queen defends d4, so White can simply take the g-pawn, and Black must find enough activity and development to justify the pawn.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 e5.name: Borg Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 e5.strategy: Offers a central pawn: the queen now guards g5, but White simply takes on e5 and is a pawn up with the better centre. A gambit without clear compensation.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4.strategy: Attacks g5 a second time: bishop and h-pawn against the lone h6 pawn. It forces Black to act, but it advances a rook's pawn before any piece is out and loosens White's own kingside; developing is the calmer way to keep the edge.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 g4.name: Borg Defence: Troon Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 g4.strategy: Pushes the attacked pawn instead of defending it, but nothing protects it on g4: the queen takes it at once. Black gets a few tempi against the queen for a pawn, which is not enough.

1.e4 h5 2.d4 Nf6.name: Goldsmith Defence: Picklepuss Defence
1.e4 h5 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing reply, which hits e4. Black does not make up for the tempo spent on h5, and White keeps the centre and a pleasant edge.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 e5.name: Carr Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 h6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open the centre at once, but Black has not a single piece out. After the pawn is taken, White has an extra pawn and the lead in development, and open lines favour the side ahead in development.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4, which the knight on c3 defends, and develops. White cannot push the e-pawn to gain space with tempo, as the knight on c6 would simply take it. Black gets an ordinary developed position and White chooses the set-up.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 e6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: French Connection
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn structure, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn, so the usual break against White's centre is missing. Playable, but Black has made a harder version of the structure for itself.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. The knight on c6 is committed early, and White can build a full pawn centre without hindrance; Black must wait for a chance to challenge it.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: A compact defence: the pawn controls e5, opens the bishop on c8 and keeps Black's position sound. Black concedes the centre without attacking it, so White gets space and the choice of plans, and Black waits for a chance to challenge later.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and invites White to push the pawn and gain space with tempo, in the hope of undermining the advanced pawn later. The knight already on c6 adds little to that plan, and White gets the space at no cost.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Franco-Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Builds a solid pawn structure and prepares ...d5, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn and takes away the usual break against White's centre. Playable, though White gets a freer game than in the normal version of the structure.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Colorado Countergambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.background: Played with some success by the American international master Doug Root and more recently by the Finnish IM Olli Salmensuu, among others. Eric Schiller, who also calls it the Lean Variation, describes it as "fierce" and for "thrill-seekers".
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Strikes at e4 from the flank, hoping to open lines and get ...d5 in. It weakens Black's own king, and White can simply take the pawn. Black can usually win the material back, but pays for it with a permanently loosened kingside.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Colorado Countergambit Accepted
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn, which also removes the e-pawn from the centre. Black cannot recapture at once, so the choice is whether to hold the extra pawn or hand it back for a comfortable game. The f-pawn is gone for good, so Black's kingside stays weakened.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Gains space and attacks the knight in one move. The pawn is attacked by the knight on c6 and guarded by Nf3, so White gets a central space advantage that Black must try to undermine, or else be cramped.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.background: Invented by the Spanish grandmaster Marc Narciso Dublan, who called it "El Columpio" ("The Swing").
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight again to hit e5 a second time. The idea is risky: White guards the pawn with a central move, and the knight, which has moved twice, will probably end up on the rim while White keeps the space and an edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn, so that it is guarded by pawn and knight against the two attackers. White builds a strong pawn centre, and Black's knight has used up its time.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6.strategy: Attacks e5 a third time, with knight, knight and pawn, and opens the c8-bishop. White's advanced pawn is now attacked three times and guarded twice, so White must act at once, and Black has found the real point of the knight's journey.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Chases the knight and so removes one of the three pieces attacking e5. White spends a pawn move on it but gains time, because the knight has to go to the edge of the board and Black's counterplay thins out.

The only sensible retreat: the others lose the knight or give it up for a pawn. It stands on the rim, but it still covers f5 and f7, and the pressure on e5 remains. Black has to accept a slightly worse position.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, Exchange Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Removes the attacked pawn by exchange and so eases the tension in the centre. Black's recapture leaves a simple position where the knight on h6 is still misplaced, and White keeps a small, stable edge in space and development.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, Pin Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Pins the knight on c6 against the king, so it cannot move. This takes it out of the fight for e5 and d4, and the bishop can capture it and double Black's pawns. White keeps the better pawn centre and the initiative.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, El Columpio Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Offers a pawn to open lines for the pieces. It can simply be taken, leaving Black a clean pawn up, and White's compensation is little more than the bishop on c1 aimed at the knight on h6 to damage Black's kingside pawns.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and attack White's centre from a distance. It is a sound set-up, but the knight on h6 is misplaced and White has gained space, so Black plays a worse version of a flank defence.
